Snyk.author: skellertor
Snyk.title: Show HN: DOM-defense – turn your current webpage into a tower defense level
Snyk.text: I kept thinking about how a lot of us have to be online to do our work each day. It is not uncommon to have other open tabs with social media, games, or whatever. Why not turn your current page, whatever site you are on, into a game?So I built DOM-defense. Once you click play on the current tab and it overlays a tower-defense game on that page. The path snakes its way through the pages hyperlinks. You place towers in the empty space. Enemies march alont the path and if they break the last blockade, you lose. Survive 100 waves and you win.A couple of details that mattered to me while building it:Variety - Every page is a different map (news, docs, Wikipedia, whatever). You are not confined to set levels. Every site is different so it naturally creates infinite varietyWork within a users current flow - Instead of opening other tabs or another site, I wanted a user to not have to "go outside" of their normal workflowDifficulty/Fun factor - I spent some time tuning it to make it difficult, but beatable. Finding the balance is difficult when a user can literally play it on any siteIt’s free on the Chrome Web Store:https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dom-defense/bglbhkd...Curious what pages break it hardest, or what would make the loop more fun. Happy to answer any questions too.

Snyk.author: frumiousirc
Snyk.text: I've used org-babel in big and small contexts for more than a decade. I generally reach for the patter for a few goals:- Keep diagram source (eg Graphviz dot) with the document.- Write software developer manuals that can reference code robustly as the code changes (eg include code snippets from source based on regex).- Literate Coding / Reproducible Research pattern. Eg, org file explains and generates/builds/runs code and graphs/figures which then get included back into the document.Some of the problems- At some scale, one needs a DAG (eg make) or to make every command idempotent with fast no-op. Otherwise, each little change to a source block takes too long and there is a worry that something didn't update which should.- At some scale, the document becomes the size of a library/package and it does not compose and/or I want to run the code outside of the document.- The unenlightened around me do not use Emacs so an org file is a "me" file. In some ways this is a plus as it keeps others fingers out of my pie but it also means no way to share the baking.That was in the days before LLMs. As ellieh's #3 points out, things are different now (we all know that). I now have an LLM externalize org-babel. The LLM maintains an org or LaTeX document describing bits of work, an external library/CLI which runs to produce content including putting numerical results into LaTeX macros, a Makefile or Snakemake to regenerate content and figures. When things are found to change prior understanding the LLM remakes a section of prose in the LaTeX document. I then write my own notes or another LaTeX document so that the trip through eyeballs to fingers on the keyboard assures I keep some level of understanding.Likewise, in the software documentation goal, it's far better to give a good LLM access to the source and have it generate documentation targeting some learning goal with follow exploration via Q&A than it is to read some prepared document that assumes my goal. Software documentation is kind of a relic useful only for those people that have not yet taken up LLM tools.

Semgrep.author: cauch
Semgrep.text: > I just searched for effects of tracking on high performing students.What are the first results you get? I get an article on "engagement" (which is not really the subject), then a study that conclude "The results suggest that early tracking increases educational inequality. While less clear, there is also a tendency for early tracking to reduce mean performance." (aka dragging everyone to the bottom)I find it surprising that you've only found studies that show tracking to be beneficial.> Also the meta-analysis you posted basically just says that a bunch of these studies have methodological flaws and don't really show anything.And those are not accounted in the conclusion that is still that mixed classroom is preferred over non-mixed ones.> And again, you have to use logic here. If you don't teach kids, but still take up their time not teaching them, how are they going to learn things?That's a fallacy. Mixing classroom is not equal to "not teaching them". Again, you said yourself that a good fraction of the class is high performance kids. 20% is a big fraction, it's 5 students over 20. You decide to frame the situation as if a good fraction was just 100% ignored, which is just you framing the situation so the conclusion is what you want to hear.> The position you're putting forward is absurd. Literally illogical. Cannot happen.Reality does not care about your feelings. The reality is what we measure when we measure the facts. This is what these studies have done. They have concluded that your naive logic is incorrect: they have measured that non-mixed classroom does not mean high performance students stop learning.> ... and I think you'll find I said that I think the smart kids would thrive if you just put them in a room with each other with some educational toys/games, and maybe gave them about a half hour of instruction per day.And this is probably exactly why mixed classroom don't damage high performing students. You are adamant to pretend that in a classroom of 20% of high performance students, the teachers will lock them in a dark room or only tell them exactly what they are telling the low performing students. But then you also explain that it is easy, just gave them stuffs to do and leave them alone. What you are saying is that basically you can easily care for a high performance student when they are in a mixed classroom.> The original context was about people having exactly the weird visceral reaction to tracking (or "discrimination" or segregation) that you display.Which "weird visceral reaction"? You said that non-mixed classrooms are an obvious good solution. This is a lie, this is incorrect. Even being generous and saying that "non-mixed may be a good solution", your affirmation was that "non-mixed wins with a clear margin, it is an _obvious_ solution, and people who are not convinced by it have no legitimacy for this position at all". I don't care about "discrimination", I don't care about "stopping your kid to get smart".Again, if I'm wrong, it would be SUPER EASY for you: articles like the ones I've provided should simply not exist. If I'm wrong, those articles are IMPOSSIBLE. If indeed non-mixed classrooms are the obvious solution you pretend it to be, every single study should either say "too large uncertainty to conclude anything" or "clear benefice from non-mixed classrooms". The fact that there are studies that say "statistically significant no benefice from non-mixed classrooms" is just the reality telling you that "it's an obvious solution" is not true.> The fact that you think it's unfulfilling to learn at the pace you're capable of instead of being made to artificially sit and wait is more of a statement about you.How being in a mixed classroom suddenly stop your kid to learn at the pace she like? YOU SAID IT YOURSELF that she needs half-hour a day of attention per day for this to be satisfied.This sentence was there where you went all crazy about "those devil people who want to force my smart kid to not be smart" or "those devil people who want all children to be the same, for some reason that no one knows". WHY? WHO IS DOING THAT? You seems to think that people cares about your kid learning or not, and try to stop her learning. That's why I pictured you as obsessed with competition: you assume that kid education is somehow a competition (otherwise there is no reason at all for other people to try to stop your kid to learn).> And, yes, my kid is an outlier, as are these other kids I'm talking about.I meant: your kid is an outlier amongst the high performance kids. No kid is the same. No high performance kid is the same. Some will need half-hour a day, some will need five hours. Some will to work out the problem by themselves, some will need guidance. Some will need to learn continuously on a long period of time, some will need scheduled short sessions with big pause in between.And you may have talked to tens of parents. 1. that is still a ridiculous small sample to drive any conclusion. 2. based on this conversation (for example how you find reason to convince yourself that your kid is in reality smarter than other kids), I'm pretty sure you heard what you wanted to hear from these parents.> Did you miss the part where ... Do you understand what ...Calm down, there. I was talking about your kid being an outlier amongst the group of high performing kids. You keep coming up with "my kid don't need more resource, so if someone says HP need more resource, they are lying", "my kid was fine with half-hour of teaching, so that is what a HP kid needs", ... And again, I'm sure you will say that you have discussed that with tens of other parents. Again, tens of parents is NOTHING. It's ANECTODICAL.But, hey, thanks for showing your true colour: I was talking of your kid being an outlier amongst the HP kids, but you did not hesitate one second to come at me blaming me for something that I did not do at all.> The school knows this, and doesn't attempt to accommodate it.It may be the case, but there are a lot of as equally probable hypothesis.For example: Your kid is used to homeschooling and struggle to adapt to a classroom. Because you cannot conceive that the problem is not the result to your imaginary "bad people who, for reason no one can explain, want to stop children learn", you just jumped to the conclusion "they don't accommodate it, I'm so much smarter than them, let me come with a genius idea". Then, you met the teachers and proposed ideas that people who have tried noticed will not work, and you got angry when they politely discarded them (instead of thinking that maybe they know things you don't, you just assumed you are so much better than them). Then, you talked to other parents, some of them in the same crazy state as you, some of them indulging you, some of them probably trying to balance your position but you did only hear what suits you.All of that fits very well all the data points. Way more that the hypothesis that, despite the fact that your kid is so easy to teach for and that it will benefit mainly to all the other kids, somehow people refused your idea.

Semgrep.author: ndriscoll
Semgrep.text: I just searched for effects of tracking on high performing students. I'm not sure how you could ever quantify what's easier to find, but sure. Also the meta-analysis you posted basically just says that a bunch of these studies have methodological flaws and don't really show anything.And again, you have to use logic here. If you don't teach kids, but still take up their time not teaching them, how are they going to learn things? The position you're putting forward is absurd. Literally illogical. Cannot happen. Like, yeah, if you don't let anybody take calculus, their math grades might go up. Because you stopped asking anything of them. They might also feel more confident? Which doesn't mean a whole lot if they actually want to do university math and find out they're way behind, and their school just never actually offered anything past what other kids were doing in middle school.If you think you got a different result, the conclusion needs to be that you measured the wrong thing and you asked the wrong question.I think I've been pretty clear that it's about 20% of the kids that are apparently operating at a very high level. I've been told that the median is around the national median, which is to say abysmal. I don't have a good picture of the distribution between the 50th and 80th percentile at our school. So yes, the class is operating at a level several years beneath her. And if I assume that 20% of her cohort are above her, then it's also operating at a level years beneath them. Again, this is just a basic logical inference granting the assumption that they told me.I don't know where you get this idea about force-feeding books. I said I've never worked with her for more than about a half hour in a given day, and I think you'll find I said that I think the smart kids would thrive if you just put them in a room with each other with some educational toys/games, and maybe gave them about a half hour of instruction per day.I also never suggested I'm competing with you or anyone or that anyone is a threat? The original context was about people having exactly the weird visceral reaction to tracking (or "discrimination" or segregation) that you display. I want her to learn about the world because life is interesting. The fact that you think it's unfulfilling to learn at the pace you're capable of instead of being made to artificially sit and wait is more of a statement about you.And, yes, my kid is an outlier, as are these other kids I'm talking about. That was literally the start of the discussion. We are talking about how the score handles outliers. The statistics of our school are that the class has a large number of what would be considered outliers at the national level. Did you miss the part where I said at least 15 kids in the cohort were measured at the 99th percentile? Do you understand what percentile means? They are, by definition, outliers. Or stated that the school said my kid is at the 97th percentile on the test they gave? That's ~2.5 standard deviations. And then I threw out numbers that made it pretty clear that there are around 100 kids in the cohort. Obviously we are not a typical distribution. The school knows this, and doesn't attempt to accommodate it.And in fact, the first step for them would be to notice that their test doesn't attempt to measure the relative position of outliers. It stops at the skill it's trying to measure, which is far beneath their level. I imagine that if you or I were given a kindergarten test, we would also place above the 95th percentile, but it probably can't say very much about our relative ability because it makes no attempt to actually measure where we're at, and we're likely both well above kindergarten level.(Not that this is particularly germane to the discussion, but since you keep calling me an armchair scientist, I do actually have published work on modeling plasma physics from my undergrad. I'm familiar with science)
